title: ICJ rules on Rohingya genocide today as Dhaka seeks accountability
excerpt: The world court gives its verdict in The Gambia v Myanmar later today. Refugees in Cox's Bazar say they want justice and a safe way home.

image.alt: The Peace Palace in The Hague, seat of the International Court of Justice, seen across its front garden
image.credit: File photo: Velvet / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver its judgment in The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar today, Thursday 19 November, at a public sitting in The Hague. On the eve of the ruling, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said accountability is "essential to delivering justice to the Rohingya people", The Business Standard reported, citing UNB.

She made the remarks on 18 November when she met Kelley Currie, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, at the foreign ministry. She said Bangladesh is following the judgment closely, called repatriation "the only viable and durable solution", and urged a coordinated international roadmap for return. She put the number of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh at about 1.3 million.

The case

The Gambia filed the case in November 2019 under the Genocide Convention, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, Human Rights Watch (HRW) says. Eleven countries have been allowed to intervene. Hearings on the merits ended in January 2026. The court will decide whether Myanmar as a state broke the convention. It is not a criminal trial of individuals, and the judgment is final, with no appeal, HRW has noted. The court has no power of its own to enforce it.

Voices from the camps

Refugees in Cox's Bazar told bdnews24.com they want justice and repatriation. "We don't want revenge; we want justice," said Rahima Khushi, a Rohingya rights worker who has interpreted for The Gambia's legal team. Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner Mizanur Rahman told the paper the ruling could strengthen international pressure on Myanmar.

"We want to go back," Mohammad Zubair, chairman of the Arakan Rohingya Society for Peace and Human Rights, told Al Jazeera. Thomas Kean of the International Crisis Group warned that "the Arakan Army can hardly make guarantees around safety while a war is going on" in Rakhine State.

Why it matters

This is the biggest accountability moment for the Rohingya since the 2017 exodus, when more than 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh. A ruling against Myanmar would give Bangladesh and refugee groups stronger grounds to press for safe return, but it will not by itself change daily life in the camps, where aid budgets are already shrinking. NGOs should expect gatherings in the camps today and many questions from refugees about what the verdict means for them.

What to watch

The judgment itself, Myanmar's response, statements from donors and the UN Security Council, and whether the verdict brings new funding pledges for the 2027 response.
